title: Total Characters in String After Transformations II
statement:
`s` is a string of lowercase letters, `t` is a number of rounds, and `nums` holds 26 integers, one per letter of the alphabet (`nums[0]` belongs to `'a'`, `nums[25]` to `'z'`).

In one round, every letter of the current string is replaced, all at the same time, by the `nums[c]` letters that come right after it in the alphabet, in alphabetical order, where `c` is the letter's index (`'a'` is 0). The alphabet is circular: the letter after `'z'` is `'a'`.

After exactly `t` rounds, report how many letters the string has. That count can be enormous, so return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
signature: int lengthAfterTransformations(String s, int t, List<Integer> nums)
notes:
## Intuition

The string grows up to 25-fold per round, so it can never be built. It also does not need to be: every copy of the same letter turns into the same letters, so the 26 letter counts are all that matter. One round maps those counts linearly: a letter `x` adds its count to each of the `nums[x]` letters after it. Write that map as a 26 × 26 matrix `transition` and `t` rounds become `counts × transition^t`.

Simulating round by round costs about 26 · 25 · t steps, hopeless for t = 10^9. A matrix power, like a number power, comes from repeated squaring: O(26³ · log t), with every entry kept modulo 10^9 + 7.

## Approach

1. Build `transition`: row `letter` has a 1 in the column of each of the `nums[letter]` letters after it, wrapping with `% 26`.
2. Count the letters of `s` into `counts`, a matrix with a single row, so the same `multiply` serves for both products.
3. While `rounds > 0`: if its lowest bit is 1, apply the current power with `counts = multiply(counts, transition)`. Then square `transition`, which now stands for twice as many rounds, and halve `rounds`.
4. `multiply` is the ordinary matrix product, reducing every entry modulo `MOD`.
5. Return the sum of the final counts modulo `MOD`.

## Example 1, step by step

`counts` holds 1 each for `a`, `b`, `c` and 2 for `y`. Each row of `transition` maps a letter to the next one, except `z`, which becomes `a` and `b`. `t = 2` is binary `10`: the low bit is 0, so `transition` is only squared into the two-round map (`a` to `c`, `y` to `a` and `b`, `z` to `b` and `c`). The next bit is 1, so `counts` is multiplied by it, giving one each of `c`, `d`, `e` and two each of `a` and `b`: 7 letters, as in `"cdeabab"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + 26³ · log t): counting reads `s` once, and each of the about 30 halvings does at most two 26 × 26 products.
- Space: O(26²) for the matrices.

## Pitfalls

- A product of two residues reaches about 10^18, beyond 2^53: use `BigInt` (or `long` with `%` after each product in Java and C).
- Keep the orientation: `transition[from][to]` with `counts` as a row on the left. Transposing it describes the reverse process.
- Forgetting `% 26` sends `z` and its neighbours to letters that do not exist.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | 10^9 + 7 as a `BigInt` |
| `transition` | `transition[x][y]`: copies of `y` that one `x` becomes over the rounds it stands for (1, 2, 4, ...) |
| `counts` | one-row matrix: how many of each letter the string holds so far |
| `rounds` | rounds still to apply; its bits choose which powers are used |
| `row`, `out` | a row of `a` and the matching row of the product |
| `total` | sum of the final counts |

narration.2: Answers are taken modulo the prime 10^9 + 7; BigInt keeps the 10^18-sized products exact.
narration.4: multiply(a, b) is the ordinary matrix product, done one row of a at a time.
narration.6: This will become the matching row of the product.
narration.7: row[k] is the amount this row holds of letter k...
narration.8: ...and row k of b says how many of each letter j one k turns into.
narration.9: Add row[k] * b[k][j]; BigInt has no overflow, so reduce only once per entry.
narration.12: Reduce each entry modulo MOD before it is used again.
narration.16: transition[x][y] will say how many y's one x becomes in a round.
narration.18: A letter turns into the nums[letter] letters after it...
narration.22: counts is a one-row matrix, so multiply can apply transition to it.
narration.26: Square-and-multiply: handle one bit of t per pass, halving rounds each time.
narration.27: Is the lowest remaining bit set?
narration.28: Then apply the current power of transition to the letter counts.
narration.30: Square transition: it now covers twice as many rounds.
narration.32: The string length is the sum of the 26 letter counts.
narration.33: Reduce once more and return an ordinary number.
